articles.title: Andrew Griffith to unveil Tory plans to cut taxes and regulations
articles.summary: Shadow ministers will unveil a series of policies on day two of the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.
articles.body:
Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith is to outline his plans for the UK economy, including hopes to cut taxes, red tape and house-building costs.

Griffith and his colleagues will use day two of the party's conference in Birmingham to also explain how they would want to reduce food costs, support Heathrow Airport expansion and abolish Natural England and the Environment Agency.

Another prospective policy is replacing agreements designed to compel developers to fund community projects and services in areas they want to build.

Griffith will describe his approach as the "most ambitious deregulation project in a generation". Reform UK suggested the Tories were "copying our policies".

Griffith's speech comes after Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch published a 100-page document explaining her guiding principles and how her party would act should it return to government by winning the next general election.

Following their historic defeat in the 2024 general election, the Conservatives have been trying to rebuild and convince voters that they can be trusted again.

The Tories have faced repeated attacks from their opponents for their record in government, including on the economy, between 2010 and 2024.

Griffith is expected to say: "No-one else is coming to save our economy. Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation."

He will accuse Prime Minister Andy Burnham of wanting to pursue a "socialist fever dream of the 1970s", adding the Tories want to deliver "cheaper homes, lower taxes, and less red tape".

Chancellor John Healey last week said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" and the Budget on 28 October would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space".

During a series of speeches on Monday, Conservative shadow ministers will continue to make their case and provide more details of their proposals.

This will include ditching environmental and energy efficiency regulations, including the future homes standard.

The Tories believe their changes could cut the cost of delivering a new home by up to £50,000, which in turn they expect could save money for buyers.

A single levy for developers would be implemented in place of section 106 agreements and the Community Infrastructure Levy, which fund projects in the community when building plans are progressed.

The Conservatives argue this new charge would remove delays and improve how the funds are spent to the benefit of residents.

The party has been critical of the roles of Natural England and the Environment Agency in relation to house building and flood prevention work respectively, and wants to abolish both. Their functions would be looked after by the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra).

The Extended Packaging Responsibility (EPR) scheme, which requires firms to cover the cost of collecting, recycling and disposing of packaging it produces, would also be scrapped by the Conservatives.

The party believes this would help lift a "burden" from businesses and in turn could cut the cost of the weekly shop.

On Heathrow, Griffith is expected to say the next Conservative government would do "whatever it takes to end the delays and boost capacity by backing the third runway".

Plans for expansion were scrapped by the Tory-led coalition government in 2010.

Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves championed the runway to boost the economy after Labour won power, although Burnham has refused to say whether he backs the project since becoming prime minister.

Burnham has described it as "principally... a matter for London and Londoners".

Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the Conservatives have "cemented their position as a pointless anti-growth anti-business party" by rejecting closer ties with Europe.

She added: "No-one can take anything the Conservatives say on the economy seriously given their litany of fantasy-land financial pledges."

Reform UK economy spokesman Robert Jenrick accused the Conservatives of "once again copying our policies".

articles.title: Russia threatens more strikes after Zelensky vows to hit oil refineries
articles.summary: The Russian Defense Ministry on Sunday threatened to hit Ukrainian military and industrial facilities, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his military would target Russia’s oil refineries. “Strikes by the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation against military and military-industrial facilities, as well as related infrastructure in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine, will be…
articles.body:
The Russian Defense Ministry on Sunday threatened to hit Ukrainian military and industrial facilities, after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his military would target Russia’s oil refineries.

“Strikes by the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation against military and military-industrial facilities, as well as related infrastructure in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine, will be intensified,” the defense ministry wrote on Telegram, as reported by Politico .

“The people of Ukraine should blame only the head of the Kyiv regime for this,” the ministry added, referring to Zelensky. “It is [Zelensky] who bears full personal and political responsibility for this.”

Zelensky told Reuters on Saturday his armed forces will continue to target Russian oil refineries in response to the invading country’s wave of airstrikes.

The Ukrainian president added his intelligence services have obtained documents showing that Russian President Vladimir Putin has issued guidance for his military to broaden its attacks on civilian targets ahead of the winter.

“We saw documents ‌and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals,” Zelensky told Reuters. “To pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities: this is the goal of the operation.”

While President Trump has enlisted special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, his son-in-law, to broker peace between Putin and Zelensky, the two have so far failed to do so.

Last month, Zelensky said Trump greenlit Ukraine building Patriot missiles. The Ukrainian leader, whose country is in its fifth year of its war against Russia, has repeatedly asked his American counterpart for authorization to construct the missiles to protect itself against Kremlin missile and drone strikes.

Russian strikes killed more Ukrainian civilians over the first eight months of this year than all of last year, according to the United Nations (U.N.). Last month, Russian attacks killed at least 372 Ukrainian civilians and injured at least 2,349, the U.N. reported.

articles.title: George Takei and his husband are giving their $21 million-plus estate to a museum; the Star Trek actor will preserve Japanese American stories
articles.summary: For George Takei, the Japanese American National Museum has been part of his life for more than four decades.
articles.body: For George Takei, the Japanese American National Museum has been part of his life for more than four decades. Now, he and his husband, Brad Takei, have arranged for their estate, currently valued at more than $21 million, to go to the museum after their deaths, as reported by the Japanese American National Museum (JANM). The planned gift will support the institution that has preserved Japanese American history while also documenting Takei’s own experiences of wartime incarceration, activism and public life. Part of the museum’s renovated core exhibition will carry the couple’s names in recognition of their support. Their decision also extends a relationship that has already seen the Takeis give millions of dollars to JANM and place much of George Takei’s personal archive in its care.George and Brad Takei pledge their $21 million estate to JANMThe Takeis have pledged to leave their estate to the Japanese American National Museum as its sole beneficiary. The estate is currently valued at more than $21 million, according to the museum, and the planned bequest is intended to provide support well beyond their lifetimes.Their connection with JANM goes back to the institution’s early years. Takei has been involved since the museum was founded in 1985 and became one of its founding trustees. He chaired its Board of Trustees between 2000 and 2004 and remains on the board.Since 1989, George and Brad Takei have given $22.5 million to JANM, with the estate commitment included in that figure.JANM names its new 9,200-square-foot gallery after the TakeisThe museum is recognising the couple’s support by naming its new 9,200-square-foot gallery after them. The gallery forms part of JANM’s redesigned core exhibition, In the Future We Call Now: Realities of Racism, Forging Democracy.The exhibition draws together Japanese American history with material relating to racism, incarceration, democracy and civic participation.Images from his personal collection are used in several parts of the exhibition. One shows Takei with his kindergarten class at the Rohwer concentration camp in Arkansas, where he was incarcerated with his family during the Second World War. Another depicts his family at the Tule Lake Segregation Center.There is also a photograph from George and Brad Takei’s wedding at JANM, linking the museum’s historical material with Takei’s later activism and public life.George Takei donated a 175-foot archive to JANM in 2017Takei was a child when his family was forced into the US wartime incarceration system. He spent time at Rohwer and later at Tule Lake, experiences that have shaped much of his work as an author and activist. Those memories have appeared in his graphic memoir They Called Us Enemy and his children’s book My Lost Freedom. They are also represented in the museum’s collections and exhibitions.In 2017, Takei donated a large personal archive to JANM. The George Takei Collection covers more than 175 linear feet and contains photographs, letters, scripts, awards, campaign material and other objects from different periods of his life.Some items are particularly connected to his family history. Among them is a sculpture made by Takei’s father while the family was held at Rohwer. The collection also contains the walking stick Takei used while climbing Mount Fuji and the Olympic torch he carried ahead of the 1984 Summer Olympic Games in Los Angeles. The archive became the basis for JANM’s 2017 exhibition New Frontiers: The Many Worlds of George Takei.George Takei’s personal record helps illustrate Japanese American historyThe museum has used Takei’s photographs to illustrate several different periods and themes. In the section dealing with life inside the camps, his kindergarten photograph helps show how schools were established for children within the ten incarceration sites.The material concerning Tule Lake places the Takei family within the larger experience of Japanese American families who were sent there. Elsewhere, his later work is used to explore how Japanese Americans have participated in public life and activism.Takei also wrote the foreword for the catalogue accompanying the new exhibition. His relationship with the museum extends beyond donations and governance, and his own historical record has become part of the material through which visitors encounter that history.JANM’s new StoryFiles preserve wartime memoriesJANM is also preparing a new way for visitors to hear directly from people who experienced the wartime camps. In March 2026, the museum previewed four new interactive StoryFiles featuring Takei and three other Japanese Americans who were incarcerated during the war.The StoryFiles were created from hours of recorded interviews. Visitors can interact with the digital presentations in a format designed to resemble a conversation, allowing personal accounts to sit alongside the museum’s physical collections.Takei’s StoryFile was produced by JANM and the National Japanese American Memorial Foundation, with the project created alongside the nonprofit Japanese American Stories. The Freeman Foundation supports the project, while Joanne Watanabe Erceg supports the StoryFile of George Takei.When JANM reopens on January 23, 2027, the new StoryFiles will be housed in the Hirasaki National Resource Center and Weingart Foundation Foyer. The StoryFile of Lawson Ichiro Sakai will also be presented there.JANM’s $135 million campaign grows alongside redevelopmentThe reopening will follow a renovation of the museum’s galleries, giving visitors new ways to encounter material covering Japanese American history. The Takei collection, his recorded testimony and the wider museum archive will sit within that expanded presentation.For Takei and Brad, the estate pledge gives the museum a future financial connection to their lives as well as to the objects and stories George has already entrusted to it. The couple’s wedding photographs, George’s childhood records and his later work are already part of the museum’s interpretation of Japanese American history. The planned estate gift also comes as JANM’s wider fundraising effort has grown substantially. The Our Promise campaign has now raised $135 million, more than twice its original target.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Cornell rape accuser receives threats, and poll shows Latino voters dropping Trump: Weekend Rundown
articles.summary: The woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted by Cornell University fraternity members has received threats pressuring her to drop her lawsuit, her attorney said.
articles.body: The woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted by Cornell University fraternity members has received threats pressuring her to drop her lawsuit, her attorney said. Thomas Giuffra told CNN’s “State of the Union” that people attempting to unmask his client’s identity had also targeted at least three women mistakenly identified as her. The former Cornell student is identified as Jane Doe in court documents. Doe filed a lawsuit last month against Cornell and seven Chi Phi fraternity members, alleging she was sexually assaulted over the course of hours on Oct. 19 and 20, 2024, while she was under the influence of ketamine, alcohol and marijuana. The suit has sparked renewed scrutiny of how the university and local authorities handled the allegations. Gov. Kathy Hochul last week appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to consider whether criminal charges are appropriate. More Cornell news: 2024 investigation: Cornell police spoke to witnesses and received anonymous tips about an alleged gang rape at a fraternity house in the first weeks of its investigation two years ago. But the local prosecutor did not review the additional information before deciding not to bring charges.Arrest at Chi Phi: Police records also show that university police made a drug-related arrest at a fraternity house 22 hours before the woman alleged she was drugged and sexually assaulted there.President’s statement: Michael Kotlikoff said in a video message Saturday that what Doe alleges is “deeply disturbing” and raises questions about the investigation that followed. Notable quote As the Cornell case continues to draw national attention, parents online are sharing how they’re teaching their children to challenge a culture that allows sexual violence to persist. Poll: Latino voters swing away from Trump and Republicans Latino voters helped propel Donald Trump back to the White House. Now, they are turning on him, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll — a shift that gives Democrats a major opportunity to capitalize in midterm elections that could hinge on states and districts with sizable Latino populations. Like the broader electorate, Latino voters are racked by major concerns about high prices and Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement. The president’s approval rating sits at 27% among Latino voters. Two-thirds say his administration’s deportation policies have gone too far, and three-quarters disapprove of how he has handled the economy and the cost of living. And Democrats have a 24-point lead on whom Latino voters want to see in control of Congress, 59%-35%. ‘Meet the Press’ Former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel called on Democratic lawmakers to set aside plans to impeach President Donald Trump if they win a majority in the House, pushing them instead to pass an ethics reform package. Asked directly on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” whether Democrats should take up impeachment in January if they take the House gavel, Emanuel said: “Short answer: No, because it’s not going anywhere, and it’s going to be a food fight, and it’s just going to be we return to the politics of fighting.” Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said in a separate “Meet the Press” interview that he is considering a run for president in 2028. “My plans right now are to run for re-election, but as I’ve said before, if I don’t think I can be effective in the Senate anymore, I would consider it,” Kennedy said. Politics in brief ‘Get out and vote’: Trump rallied Saturday for Republicans in Ohio’s competitive races for Senate and governor, predicting that the party will defy expectations in a choppy midterm election climate.‘The elephant in the room’: The estranged wife of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton urged voters to stand behind all Republicans in a new ad, though she neglected to name Paxton directly.‘Call Tom on his cellphone’: Trump appeared to share Sen. Tom Cotton’s cellphone number in a social media post about the stalled daylight saving bill. Search for 6 aboard medical jet enters second day after crash near Nantucket Authorities declined to speculate on what caused a medical evacuation jet to crash off the coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts, on Saturday morning, as crews continue to search for the six missing passengers. The U.S. Coast Guard found a debris field approximately 20 miles off the coast of Nantucket. Crews have searched roughly 2,840 square miles over more than 53 hours, said Rear Adm. Matt Lake, commander of the Coast Guard’s Northeast District. “This is a large and demanding search area. Our crews are employing fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, boats and cutters to search the area,” Lake said. He added that authorities hope to use sonar to search the seabed. The six people on board were four Canadians and two Bermudians. A source familiar with the matter told NBC News the Bermudians were a patient and the patient’s son. Governor says Tennessee’s prisons chief is resigning after failed execution of Christa Pike The head of Tennessee’s prison system is resigning after the failed execution of Christa Pike, Gov. Bill Lee announced Saturday. In response to the resignation news, Pike’s attorneys told NBC News that Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada’s departure was “justified, but it does nothing to help Christa now.” “What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person,” they said. Pike remained unconscious in a hospital as of Friday. Pike has remained unconscious and on a ventilator at a hospital in the four days since her failed execution in Tennessee, and her prognosis might not be known for days more, one of her lawyers said Sunday. Taylor Swift pops into ‘SNL’ to joke around with host Dakota Johnson Pop music icon Taylor Swift made a surprise appearance on “Saturday Night Live,” joining her friend and the episode’s host, Dakota Johnson, for some laughs. Swift appeared onstage during Johnson’s opening monologue to address her role as the movie star’s “literal therapist,” in Johnson’s words. The pop star made another appearance during the curtain call, bringing out a blue and white cake for Johnson’s birthday. In case you missed it Early indications suggest the Flydubai co-pilot accused of attacking his captain and trying to seize control of an Israel-bound plane acted alone, multiple U.S. officials briefed on the investigation and a former Israeli security official told NBC News. A dual U.K.-Iranian national arrested on suspicion of plotting a terror attack following a security incident at a U.S.-run military base in England has been released on bail, authorities said.Yemen’s Houthis say they attacked an Aramco oil facility in Riyadh with missiles and drones.A 12-year-old girl was killed and three other people were injured when gunfire erupted amid an apparent dispute over parking at a Baltimore park Saturday, officials said.

articles.title: Democracy in peril as voters illegally ousted: Former SC judge Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Ahead of a Supreme Court hearing Monday on the SIR controversy and a plea seeking suspension of the CEC for his \"unilateral decisions\", former
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Ahead of a Supreme Court hearing Monday on the SIR controversy and a plea seeking suspension of the CEC for his "unilateral decisions", former SC judge Justice Rohinton Fali Nariman Sunday flagged "malfunctioning" of the poll panel and said a citizen's right to vote, which is at the heart of democracy, was in great peril because of "illegal knocking out" of people from voters' lists.Justice Nariman also highlighted the problem in the appointment process of election commissioners, which is in Centre's hands. He expressed hope SC would rise to the occasion and rectify the mistakes prevailing in the system.He said around 93% of adjudicated cases of deleted voters in West Bengal had been decided in their favour which meant they were illegally removed. TOI had first reported on September 20 that appellate tribunals had upheld deletion of only 8,649 voters out of the 1.2 lakh cases decided so far."Now, the unfortunate part is that all this came before the court very recently. Two judges differed, and the ultimate thing is now it has gone before a bench, probably of five judges, in order to find out whether this is good law or not... But meanwhile, these appointments continue only in the hands of govt of the day. Now, we saw the danger of this happening very recently. All of you have seen that in the Bengal elections, 90 lakh voters were disenfranchised. That is an astounding figure. Ninety lakh voters getting disenfranchised did not somehow move Supreme Court enough to stay this," Justice Nariman said.Out of those who were disenfranchised, around 22 lakh filed appeals, the former SC judge said, adding, "The others must be people who don't have the wherewithal or access to justice."Justice Nariman pointed out that of 1 lakh appeals, almost all were decided in favour of the voters. "So, you can imagine this was completely illegal - knocking out of the common man, the citizen of India in order that a govt obtains what it wants. And in Bengal, we saw it ousted govt of the day and brought in govt of Centre. Now, these are very, very disturbing things that are happening in our country today," he said, speaking on 'The Constitution and the Common Man' at Rajkumar College, Rajkot."I hope the apex court, the institution to which I once belonged, steps in immediately and rectifies these things. You can't have an EC which functions or malfunctions like this. So the first important red flag qua the Constitution and the common man is the appointment process of election commissioners. The sooner the constitution bench decides you have to have somebody like a PM, leader of the opposition coupled with the Chief Justice or his nominee, who then picks the best names in order to see that votes actually translate into what they were supposed to translate into happens," Justice Nariman said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: The sexual abuse of disabled residents that shocked South Korea
articles.summary: The BBC spoke to one of three residents at a care home who were sexually assaulted by a staff member.
articles.body:
"I was hurting inside, so I came to tell my story."

These were Seo Mi-hyeon's first words to the police.

Seo, who has an intellectual disability, struggles to form long sentences and can only communicate through brief words and gestures. But her memories of the abuse inflicted upon her were clear.

She was one of three residents at a state-run care home in South Korea who were sexually assaulted by the home's director, in a case that has shocked the country and raised serious questions about state care for the disabled.

Earlier this month, a court in Seoul sentenced the director - who has only been identified by his surname Kim - to 15 years in prison. Kim is appealing the conviction.

The court had heard that some residents were made to call the director "Dad", which prosecutors said illustrated the unequal relationship between Kim and those in his care.

The ruling came nearly two years after Seo, who is in her 40s, first disclosed the abuse to her mother.

We have changed Seo's name and the names of another victim in this story to protect their identities.

Seo first began living in Saekdongwon, a care home for the intellectually disabled, in 2016.

The institute, located in the city of Incheon, is fully subsidised by the state and still houses some 33 residents, although it has been asked to close down in light of this case.

According to Seo, the abuse began shortly after she began living there, with Kim visiting her at night or in the early hours of the morning to rape her.

Speaking through her lawyer Ko Eun-young, Seo said there was no adult at the facility she could speak to about the abuse, adding that she felt that other staff members would not help her. The care home has not responded to this allegation.

That was her life for almost 10 years, until the case came to light in February 2025, when Seo suffered a head injury.

She said it happened one of the times Kim tried to sexually assault her. She had blocked him with her hands, causing him to throw a glass at her.

Her lawyer told the court that the care home took Seo to hospital and informed her mother about the incident only after the wound on her head had been stitched up.

According to Seo's lawyer, Seo's mother had asked to see CCTV footage to establish how her daughter had been injured, but the facility refused, saying they were not authorised to release it.

As a result, her mother brought her home and decided to withdraw her from the facility. It was only after Seo was told that she would not have to return to the home that she disclosed the sexual abuse to her mum, who then reported it to the police.

"I thought it was safe to speak because I was told I didn't have to go back to Saekdongwon," Seo told the BBC via her lawyer.

When asked how she had managed on her own for so many years, she said: "I just endured it."

A police investigation into Seo's account was then widened to other residents.

They found at least two other alleged victims, including Lee Mi-Na, who said that she was also raped by Kim.

Earlier this month, a judge found all three victims' testimony credible.

He was sentenced to 15 years in jail for raping Lee and Seo, five years less than the original sentence prosecutors were asking for. He has denied all allegations and has since appealed the ruling.

For the third victim, Kim was found guilty of a lesser charge of sexual violence, with the judge saying the charge of rape against her was dropped as they could not find conclusive evidence that "force or threats [were used] that rendered the victim unable to resist".

A joint response committee made up of disability rights and other civic groups have criticsed this ruling, saying a victim's ability to resist an assault should not impact the verdict they receive.

The committee has also criticised the investigation process, saying there was a failure to identify more potential victims.

In November last year, following the initial allegations of abuse, local authorities from Ganghwa County had commissioned a team from Woosuk University to conduct an in-depth assessment of Saekdongwon's residents.

The report, which was submitted to the court as evidence, found indications that many more residents - at least 10 - could have been sexually assaulted by Kim.

But during the trial, the court did not address this finding.

According to local media reports, police had struggled to establish details of alleged abuse when interviewing residents, because most of them had severe disabilities and faced difficulties communicating. Some residents reportedly gave answers unrelated to the questions or did not respond at all.

Kim has not responded to allegations that he may have abused more residents.

Jeon Ji-su, the professor who led the Woosuk research team, told the BBC that investigators had accepted "only the accounts of people who could describe the abuse in complete sentences".

But activists said that this reliance on verbal testimony meant the police failed to recognise residents with greater communication difficulties as victims.

"If victims express their experiences differently from the way we expect, shouldn't the state make a greater effort to hear their voices?" said Baek In-seong, of Hansahoe, a counselling centre for survivors of sexual violence with disabilities.

Police have said that "while there may have been shortcomings in individual instances, these should not be taken as representative of the investigation as a whole".

Rights groups have also criticised others who have sought leniency for Kim.

Ahead of the verdict, a total of 13 petitions seeking leniency were said to have been submitted to the court. One of them, from a social welfare organisation, asked the court to take into account the defendant's "contribution to the welfare sector".

Welfare advocacy group Gyeol condemned the petitioning organisations, saying: "Past service in the welfare sector does not exempt anyone from accountability."

The judge's ruling on Kim's conviction stated that his offence was "particularly reprehensible" because "despite his professional duty to protect and support [the victims'] rights and interests and prevent abuse, he exploited the imbalance of power" with his victims to "gratify his own sexual desires".

The case has shocked many in South Korea and raised questions about why the abuse was not prevented in the first place. More shocking is that it happened despite a move in 2011 to strengthen laws to protect people with disabilities from sexual assault.

That was the year a fictional film called Dogani, based on a true story of sexual abuse at a school for deaf children, premiered. Amid intense public scrutiny and protests, the school in question was shut and tougher laws were passed as a result.

These included more specific categories of sexual offences against disabled people, harsher penalties for offences committed by facility directors and employees, and the removal of the statute of limitations for some rape offences involving disabled victims.

But in the case of Saekdongwon, the abuse persisted despite regular regular inspections by Ganghwa County, the local authority responsible for overseeing the facility.

A county official told the BBC that such inspections focused largely on paperwork, and that residents were interviewed only when specific issues arose.

The official said there had also been an external monitoring team but it had received no reports from staff, and expressed regret that the authorities had not examined the situation more closely.

Jo Ha, a representative from the national council of a counselling centre who has supported some Saekdongwon victims, said some families she had spoken to had suspected there was abuse but felt unable to raise their concerns.

Leaving a facility would mean the family has to take on all care responsibilities, as finding alternative placements is difficult.

One survey conducted through a national association of parents of people living in residential facilities for those with disabilities found that around six in 10 people who secured a place in a residential facility had waited at least three years, highlighting the difficulty of accessing appropriate care.

Professor Kim Yoon-tae, the head of Woosuk University's Institute of Cognitive Science, points out that such facilities exercise great control over residents' actions, from what they eat to where they sleep in addition to their access to healthcare and even whether or not to grant they could go outside.

And while Saekdongwon is "a landmark case" because of the scale and duration of the abuse, it is also not an isolated incident, added Jo.

In 2023, an appeals court upheld an eight-year prison sentence for a worker who raped or sexually assaulted two women with intellectual disabilities at a facility in Yeongcheon the previous year.

In a separate case in Anseong, a care home worker was recently sentenced to six years in prison for repeatedly raping a female resident with a disability in 2022.

"The violence women with disabilities experience is not an individual problem," Jo said. "It is structural violence, shaped by overlapping layers of gender, disability, institutionalisation, poverty and social isolation."

South Korea jails care home head for sexually assaulting disabled residents

Since the case came to light, South Korea's prime minister has ordered the formation of a cross-government response team, calling the incident "a grave matter that calls into question the very reason for the state's existence".

In April, the government said it had inspected 1,507 residential facilities for disabled people nationwide and identified 33 suspected cases of abuse. So far investigations have been opened into eight of them.

The government also said it would strengthen targeted inspections based on risk factors, as well as joint inspections involving local authorities, police and disability rights advocacy agencies.

Ganghwa County has ordered Saekdongwon to close and the local government has revoked the licence of the foundation that operated it.

However, the closure has been deferred until the remaining residents have been relocated and arrangements for independent living have been completed.

The local government has said it will draw up individual independent-living support plans for all 33 Saekdongwon residents. That process is still under way.

Saekdongwon has filed an administrative lawsuit challenging the revocation of its licence. It has yet to comment on Kim's conviction.

Asked what had changed most since leaving Saekdongwon, Seo said: "I just feel at peace. I'm happy every day."

She also said the best thing was being able to eat and sleep when she wanted.

What she wanted most now was "to cut ties with the director completely and never have anything to do with him again".

But, Seo added, people with disabilities still need somewhere they could feel safe.

"I hope there can be a facility without sexual violence, where disabled people like us can live in peace."

articles.title: U.S. Air Force removes all bombers from British air base targeted in a suspected terrorist plot
articles.summary: The bombers at RAF Fairford “have been re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a Pentagon official told NBC News.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Air Force has brought home all of its bombers stationed at RAF Fairford, a U.S.-run military air base in England used to strike Iran, following an investigation into a planned terrorist attack at the base. A Defense Department official told NBC News that all bombers that had been deployed to the base “have been re-deployed to their home stations in the United States.” “The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities — including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States — anywhere, anytime,” the official said. The rushed withdrawal of at least 12 bombers included several that had just arrived as part of a rotation to the base, two Pentagon officials told NBC News. Aviation watchers, such as the Military Air Tracking Alliance, have observed dozens of B-52 and B-1 bombers operating out of RAF Fairford since the opening days of the Iran war. Observers noticed a host of B-1 bombers flying out of the base Sunday. President Donald Trump is weighing options for his war on Iran — including new strikes — despite his initial promises to Americans that the campaign would last a matter of weeks. “We have decisions that I’ll make about Iran. Iran’s been decimated. So the only question is — it’ll either be the easy way, or the hard way,” Trump told reporters Saturday as he left the White House for a rally in Ohio. A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terrorist attack following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and released on bail during the investigation. British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement. American bombers have used the air base, 100 miles west of London, during decades of conflicts in the Middle East. The U.S. military still maintains a sizable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a U.S. official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and the USS Malkin Island amphibious readiness group — a group of ships that together carry over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines — are heading for the region. The official said the move could have three carriers in the region as early as the end of October.

articles.title: A South Carolina man bought a painting at Goodwill for $3, thinking it might be worth a few hundred dollars; it turned out to be a Flemish work from 1650 and sold at auction in 2012 for $190,000
articles.summary: A $3 purchase at a South Carolina Goodwill store turned into one of the most remarkable thrift-store art discoveries in recent memory.
articles.body: A $3 purchase at a South Carolina Goodwill store turned into one of the most remarkable thrift-store art discoveries in recent memory. The buyer, a former antiques dealer identified only by his middle name, Leroy, spotted an oil painting in an antique frame and assumed it might be worth a few hundred dollars. His daughter-in-law later took it to Antiques Roadshow, where appraisers revealed it was a 17th-century Flemish work from around 1650. In March 2012, the painting sold at auction in Massachusetts for $190,000, according to reporting by Mental Floss and Ksl.com.A frame that caught a trained eyeLeroy, then 81, was browsing his local Goodwill when he came across a framed still life of a dinner table.His background as a former antiques dealer gave him a practical eye for age and quality. He noticed the ornate frame and judged it to be from the 1800s, which led him to wonder whether the painting inside might also be old. He told reporters that he figured the oil painting was out of the 1800s because of the frame it was in. Based on that assessment, he estimated the frame alone might be worth about $50 and the painting perhaps another $150. That put his total expectation at a couple of hundred dollars, which was enough to justify the $3 price tag, as per the reports.The purchase was driven by instinct rather than certainty. Leroy did not know the artist, the school, or the exact date of the work. He simply recognised that the frame had value and that the painting might be worth investigating further. That curiosity set in motion a chain of events that would far exceed his original expectations.Antiques Roadshow reveals the truthAbout a year after the purchase, Leroy's daughter-in-law brought the painting to Antiques Roadshow for appraisal. The show's experts examined the work closely and offered an initial estimate of $20,000 to $30,000, a figure that already dwarfed what Leroy had paid. But the real surprise was when they dated the painting to a Flemish artist from about 1650, putting it in a far older and more important category than anyone had expected. The valuation showed the painting was from a Flemish school in Amsterdam and dated back to the 17th century. Leroy's instinct about the frame had been correct, as Flemish artwork was popular in the 1800s and the painting had been framed during that period. What he had not anticipated was that the canvas itself was more than 300 years old.The Roadshow appearance gave the painting a public platform and helped establish its provenance. Appraisers could point to stylistic features and historical context that placed the work firmly in the Flemish tradition. That credibility was essential when it came time to bring the painting to auction.From appraisal to a $190,000 hammerAfter the Roadshow appraisal, the painting was consigned to an auction house in Massachusetts for sale in March 2012. The initial estimate of $20,000 to $30,000 set a baseline for expectations, but the actual bidding far exceeded that range. When the hammer came down, the work had sold for $190,000, a figure that stunned both the consignor and observers of the sale, reported Mental Floss.The buyer was a man from Worcester, Massachusetts, according to auction records cited in coverage of the event. The sale price represented a return of more than 63,000 times the original $3 purchase price, making it one of the most dramatic thrift-store windfalls on record. Leroy described it as the biggest find he had ever had.He told reporters that he planned to split the money with his son and daughter-in-law, who had been the ones to bring the painting to Antiques Roadshow in the first place. That decision reflected the collaborative nature of the discovery, where a family member's curiosity turned a casual purchase into a life-changing event.Why Flemish still-life paintings still command high pricesThe 17th-century Flemish painting tradition is celebrated for its meticulous craftsmanship and rich symbolism. Still lifes from the era teem with food, flowers, and household objects, all rendered with extraordinary illumination and texture. Once highly prized during the Dutch Golden Age, these works continue to be much sought-after by leading museums and private collectors.This particular canvas, dating from 1650, is from the height of Flemish art, and has survived over 360 years in a condition that has allowed it to be sold at auction, helping its value as provenance and condition are key for historic works.The painting’s journey from a Goodwill store shelf to a Massachusetts auction house is proof of how easily masterworks can get lost in the annals of history. Documentation can become lost through generations, allowing high-value art to hide in plain sight until a keen eye, a curious relative and a professional appraiser team up to uncover the truth.A story that keeps thrift shoppers lookingLeroy's find is often cited alongside other famous thrift-store discoveries, including a $9.99 painting by abstract artist Ilya Bolotowsky that sold for more than $27,000 at Sotheby's in 2012. These stories fuel the hope that valuable art can still be found in everyday places. Goodwill stores and similar donation centres receive thousands of items each week, and not every donor knows the full history of what they are giving away.For collectors and casual shoppers alike, the lesson is that value is not always visible at first glance. A frame, a signature, a label, or even the quality of the canvas can be clues worth investigating. Leroy's $3 purchase is a reminder that curiosity and a willingness to look closer can sometimes pay off in ways no one expects.The $190,000 sale stands as one of the most dramatic examples of thrift-store treasure in recent years. It shows that the gap between what something appears to be worth and what it might actually fetch at auction can be enormous. For Leroy and his family, that gap turned a simple shopping trip into a story that continues to be told more than a decade later.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US withdraws B-1 bomber aircraft from UK’s Fairford base amid Iran fears
articles.summary: The abrupt redeployment to the US comes after several ‘terrorism-related’ arrests were made outside RAF Fairford.
articles.body:
The United States has made the abrupt decision to withdraw its bombers from the Royal Air Force (RAF) base Fairford in the western part of the United Kingdom, citing concerns about a potential attack.

Media reports emerged on Sunday that an urgent redeployment was under way, with B-1 bombers leaving RAF Fairford for the US.

Roughly a dozen such aircraft had been based at RAF Fairford prior to the sudden departure.

“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all US bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a Pentagon spokesperson told the Reuters news agency.

It is unclear precisely what prompted the withdrawal, which comes as the US and Israel remain embroiled in a war against Iran.

RAF Fairford has served as a stopping point for US bombers participating in the war, which began more than seven months ago, on February 28.

But the base, located roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, has been rumoured to be the target of a “terror” plot involving Iran.

On September 27, UK authorities arrested five men on suspicion of plotting to plant explosives near the base.

Iran has denied any such scheme, and the men were released without charge a day later. Investigators discovered petrol, but no explosive devices, in their vans. Still, officials in the UK say they remain under investigation.

On Thursday, British police also announced they had arrested a 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national in London on suspicion of plotting an attack against the airbase.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested last week that “Iran played a part” in the alleged plot, though he declined to provide details.

“The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry,” Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, said in a statement.

“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles — including possible foreign state involvement.”

US President Donald Trump responded to the initial arrests by accusing the men of seeking to do “big damage” to US facilities. He also praised UK authorities for their efforts.

“The arrest in the UK was fantastic. Working with Britain — it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation,” Trump said of the suspects. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them.”

Iran, meanwhile, summoned the UK ambassador to Tehran over the last week in protest of the arrests.

The US has a long history of stationing forces at RAF Fairford during its wars in the Middle East, stretching back to the Gulf War in the 1990s.

RAF Fairford has been the site of antiwar protests in the past. During one instance, in 2003, five protesters broke into the airbase in an attempt to destroy military equipment slated to be used in the US invasion of Iraq.

The UK has largely declined to participate in the ongoing war on Iran, despite pressure from the Trump administration.

Still, while the UK government was initially hesitant to let the US use its bases for the war, it granted the US “defensive” access to bases including Fairford and RAF Diego Garcia in March.

articles.title: Nicaragua says it will withdraw from Central American Parliament
articles.summary: The country’s crackdown on human rights has left it increasingly isolated in Latin America.
articles.body:
Nicaragua’s government has announced it will withdraw from the Central American Parliament, a key regional body, as President Daniel Ortega and his co-president and wife, Rosario Murillo, consolidate power.

The Foreign Ministry announced on Saturday that it would exit the six-country parliament, established to help promote human rights and democracy in Central America.

The announcement comes shortly after Friday’s passage of a resolution at the Organization of American States (OAS), calling on Nicaragua to restore civil rights and release political prisoners.

The Nicaraguan government, however, said Saturday’s action was “in the full exercise of its sovereignty”.

The government said the decision would take effect immediately, the latest in a series of withdrawals from regional and international organisations the country has undertaken.

The Ortega-Murillo government has accused such international groups of being vehicles for outside intervention .

Nicaragua pulled out of the OAS in 2023 and the United Nations Human Rights Council (UNHCR) in 2025 over criticisms of the country’s human rights record, which has deteriorated during Ortega’s tenure.

Ortega has been accused of using the state to target critics and dissidents , including through imprisonment, torture and exile.

A UN report released in September found the government was responsible for at least eight deaths in custody since 2018, when Ortega began a sharp crackdown on protests and dissent.

The report also detailed inconsistencies in the government’s account of in-custody deaths, including that of Indigenous Miskito leader Brooklyn Rivera.

A critic of the Ortega government, Rivera was detained for 32 months with minimal contact with his family before dying in May.

The government blamed his death on the effects of a previous case of COVID-19, an assessment the Physicians for Human Rights group called “not medically coherent”.

“A State that resorts to enforced disappearance and allows persons to die in its custody falls short of the minimum human rights standards required for credible democratic governance,” said Jan-Michael Simon, the group’s chair.

The administration of US President Donald Trump has also been vocal in denouncing the Nicaraguan government’s abuses, including Rivera’s death.

In July, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio published a statement calling Nicaragua’s government a “dictatorship” after it announced it would abolish the country’s upcoming elections.

He also framed the Ortega-Murillo government as a threat to US national security. “Ortega’s pledge to abolish elections in Nicaragua proves his cowardice and fear of the Nicaraguan people’s will,” Rubio wrote.

But the Trump administration has come under criticism for seeking to deport Nicaraguan citizens who were expelled under Ortega’s leadership.

Human Rights Watch recently warned that the Trump administration had detained eight Nicaraguan nationals for deportation, seven of whom were among 222 political prisoners flown into exile in the US in February 2023, during former President Joe Biden’s administration.

Nicaragua subsequently stripped them of their citizenship and branded them as “traitors” to the country. The Ortega government also seized any property they had in the country.

Human Rights Watch urged the Trump administration not to deport the eight detainees, warning that they could face abuse if they were returned to Nicaragua. Four of the detainees reportedly have pending asylum cases.

“After offering refuge to these critics of the Nicaraguan government just three years ago, the United States is now detaining and threatening to deport them,” Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at Human Rights Watch, said in a statement.

“International law prohibits the United States from returning anyone to face the threat of persecution or torture. US authorities should not be trying to send these men back into danger.”

articles.title: Portland teen faces terrorism, attempted murder charges after school cafeteria chemical scare
articles.summary: A 15-year-old Benson Polytechnic High School student faces 19 counts including domestic terrorism after allegedly mixing toxic chemicals in the cafeteria.
articles.body: An Oregon high school cafeteria chemical scare that left a student in critical condition has escalated into a domestic terrorism and attempted murder case against the same teenager school staff rushed to save. The 15-year-old Benson Polytechnic High School student faces 19 criminal counts after authorities said he brought chemicals from home and mixed them inside the Portland school Sept. 8, releasing toxic gases that endangered students and staff. "Safety in our schools is not something that can be negotiated," Multnomah County District Attorney Nathan Vasquez said during an Oct. 2 news conference. "That violence or the threat of violence in a school… it doesn't just stay in that building. It follows families home. It sits at the dinner table with them." THREE SCHOOL SAFETY STEPS EVERY PARENT SHOULD KNOW BEFORE CLASSES BEGIN Investigators uncovered "concerning behaviors and statements" before the incident, including an interest in hazardous chemicals, explosives and violence, Portland Police Bureau Public Information Manager Mike Benner said. MIDDLE SCHOOL STUDENT ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY STASHING HOMEMADE GUNS FOR ROBBERY PLOT: SHERIFF The teenager, whose name has not been released because of his age, faces 10 counts of attempted aggravated murder, one count of attempted first-degree murder, one count of attempted second-degree murder, one count of first-degree domestic terrorism and one count of second-degree domestic terrorism. Additional charges include unlawfully manufacturing and possessing a destructive device, possessing a weapon in a public building, unlawfully using a weapon and recklessly endangering another person. 15-YEAR-OLD ACCUSED OF FIRING INTO CROWD DURING DEADLY SEATTLE MASS SHOOTING CLAIMS SELF-DEFENSE The teen’s lawyers denied the allegations and said he is receiving treatment at an inpatient mental health facility, The New York Times reported. Vasquez said his office would seek to move the case from juvenile court to adult court, emphasizing the safety of the students and staff. "And I want to be clear, they're teenagers, but these are children, and they deserve a safe environment," he said. But the prosecutor sharply criticized what he called a broader failing of Oregon’s juvenile system, which ends its oversight at age 25 even if the person still poses a danger to the public. "I think that that is wrong," Vasquez said, arguing that the cutoff fails to account for the danger someone convicted of multiple killings or domestic terrorism could still present. "I'm looking at conduct and how dangerous that is and what I consider to be safe for the community going forward," he said. INJURED LOUISIANA BOY HAILED A 'SUPERHERO' FOR SEEKING HELP DURING DEADLY STABBING RAMPAGE The chemical incident unfolded shortly before 8:30 a.m. while numerous students and staff were near the teenager, Assistant Chief of Investigations Franz Schoening said. Teachers and administrators moved students away as the school nurse began treating the teen before first responders arrived. He was taken to a hospital in critical condition but survived. SUBSTITUTE TEACHER ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY TRIGGERING FALSE ACTIVE SHOOTER ALERTS AT 5 SCHOOLS: SHERIFF "Those first few moments were critical in preventing further harm and lives being lost," Schoening said. More than 100 students and staff were assessed after evacuating, and at least seven required medical care following the incident, he said. DETROIT-AREA COUPLE ACCUSED OF THROWING EXPLOSIVE DEVICE WITH ALARMING 2-WORD MESSAGE INTO NEIGHBOR'S YARD Sgt. Jim DeFrain, who supervises the investigation and the Metropolitan Explosive Disposal Unit, said initial testing indicated the presence of hydrogen sulfide, a toxic gas. An Oregon National Guard team agreed with that assessment. Samples were sent to an FBI laboratory for further testing, with results still pending at the time of the briefing, DeFrain said. The FBI was also examining electronic equipment seized during searches. Vasquez said the investigation remained open and that anyone else found to have criminal involvement could face charges. articles.title: Pentagon pulls B-1 bombers from UK base following alleged terror threat
articles.summary: The Pentagon pulled all 12 B-1 bombers this weekend from the U.K.’s RAF Fairford air base to their home stations in the U.S. weeks after an alleged terror threat against a U.S.-operated post in England. “While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now…
articles.body:
The Pentagon pulled all 12 B-1 bombers this weekend from the U.K.’s RAF Fairford air base to their home stations in the U.S. weeks after an alleged terror threat against a U.S.-operated post in England.

“While operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our assets and forces in real-time, we can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” a Pentagon official told The Hill on Sunday.

“The Airmen that operate America’s bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities – including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States – anywhere, anytime,” the official added.

Flight trackers spotted multiple B-1 bombers departing the base, located in Gloucestershire, Sunday morning.

Officials did not reveal what prompted the rushed withdrawal of the heavy, long-range bombers that can carry a payload of both guided and unguided weapons.

The U.S. military has relied on the military base to base B-52 and B-1 bombers for the Trump administration’s war against Iran.

The withdrawal comes after British authorities arrested six men linked to a suspected attack on the air base that officials said was foiled. The U.K. police have released the suspects on bail, but the investigation into the incident has continued.

Five of the men involved in the incident were U.K. nationals in their 20s. Authorities have not released names of any of the men arrested in connection with the incident.

A U.K.-Iranian dual national who was arrested was released on bail, British authorities confirmed on Saturday.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that the UK government believes that Iran “played a part” in the alleged thwarted attack on the base.

Iran has denied its involvement in a thwarted terrorist attack.

articles.title: Flydubai flight incident: Omani co-pilot may have tried to cut engines after cockpit attack
articles.summary: The Omani co-pilot who attacked the captain of a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv may have tried to crash the aircraft in the Saudi desert after
articles.body: The Omani co-pilot who attacked the captain of a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv may have tried to crash the aircraft in the Saudi desert after realising that passengers were about to thwart his attempt to seize control of the plane, according to an investigation by Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera cited by Ynet News.The report said the co-pilot, identified as Hamam al-Hammami, after repeatedly striking Indian captain Smit Machchhar with a crash axe, took control of the Boeing 737 after the injured captain activated the switch that allowed the cockpit door to be opened.Once he realised his plan to crash the aircraft would fail, he allegedly tried to bring it down in the Saudi desert.According to the investigation, the attacker disconnected the autopilot and pushed the aircraft's controls sharply forward, sending the plane into a steep descent. The aircraft lost around 16,000 feet in less than a minute.Report raises possibility engines were shut downThe Corriere della Sera investigation also raised a possibility not previously reported, that the co-pilot may have cut the fuel supply to the aircraft's engines.Two Boeing 737 captains who examined videos recorded inside the aircraft reached this possibility after noticing that the emergency lights in the passenger cabin suddenly came on during the flight, Ynet News reported.The emergency lighting is designed to assist passengers during an evacuation or when an aircraft is on the ground.
